newsitem.title: USA: Calif. quake insurance agency opens for business.
newsitem.headline: Calif. quake insurance agency opens for business.

text.p: The California Earthquake Authority (CEA) said Monday it was open for business and would immediately begin selling earthquake insurance policies in the state.

The privately financed, publicly managed agency was proposed after the devastating 1994 Northridge earthquake, which prompted many insurers to bow out of the California market to reduce their exposure to future quake losses.
The Northridge earthquake killed 60 people and caused $12.5 billion in insured losses in the Los Angeles area.
The earthquake authority was designed to end the shortage of earthquake insurance in the state and reinvigorate the market for homeowners' coverage, state officials said.
It will provide insurance coverage for earthquake damage to residential property owners, mobile home owners and renters.
The new state authority began operations Monday morning after more than a year of wrangling between state lawmakers, insurers and consumer groups.
"The CEA is open for business," said Greg Butler, the agency's interim chief executive officer.

In its first month of operation, the authority was expected to issue about 10,000 earthquake insurance policies. Once fully operational, Butler said the authority could handle up to 1.7 million earthquake policies.
The insurance policies will be written and serviced by private insurers, but the authority will issue the policy, pay earthquake claims and assume much of the risk.

The earthquake authority will be financed with premiums paid by those who buy earthquake coverage, cash from participating insurance companies, commitments from participating insurers and reinsurance, which insurers use to reduce their risks.
Proponents of the authority argued it would go a long way toward easing the shortage of coverage.

Without homeowners insurance, buyers in many cases cannot obtain mortgages to buy new homes. That has hurt the market for new homes, affecting builders and other Californians whose livelihoods are tied to the housing industry.

"Up until the actual implementation of the CEA, the homeowners market in the state had become very tight," said Jerry Davies of the Personal Insurance Federation of California, which represents insurers in the state. "(The CEA) reduces the exposure of all companies that participate. The bottom line is that it will reopen the market."
If successful, the California authority could become a prototype for similar agencies in other states, experts said.
